scenes.headline: How a shared codebook shrinks a splat file
scenes.sub: Spherical harmonics in Gaussian-Splat-Lite's RAD converter
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Centroid! Most of a splat's bytes are its view-dependent colour. Here is how one converter swaps them for a label.

scenes.text: Cluster every splat's view-dependent colour into one shared table, and store a label per splat instead of the coefficients.
scenes.say: The idea: cluster every splat's view-dependent colour into one shared table, and keep only a label per splat.

steps.say: Each splat carries forty-five signed bytes of spherical harmonics. That is most of the splat.
Weigh each splat by its area times its opacity, so big solid splats count more.
Run weighted k-means, searching only a few nearby groups of entries instead of all of them.
The entries become one shared table, written once in the first chunk.
Each splat keeps just the label of its nearest entry.

scenes.title: One splat in a RAD chunk

left.title: Per-splat SH
left.say: Stored per splat, the colour terms take forty-five of seventy-three bytes.

right.title: SH codebook
right.say: With the codebook, a four byte label replaces them, and the table is shared by every splat.

scenes.title: SH bytes per splat, train scene
scenes.say: On a real scene of about a million splats, the colour terms fall from twenty-nine point six three bytes to nine point four eight.

scenes.label: a small scene's file grows instead
scenes.say: But a small scene gets one entry per splat plus a label. Its file grew by five point three percent.

scenes.text: The table is fixed and the labels are cheap, so the saving grows with the scene.
scenes.say: The table stays the same size while the scene grows, so the bigger the scene, the more the codebook saves.

recap: Big scenes win, small ones lose
scenes.say: Shared table, one label per splat, and it pays on big scenes.
